3.2a — Projectiles: Instantiate, Fire, Destroy

Your turret knows when you are near; now it needs teeth. Spawning and firing a projectile looks complex, but it breaks down into four smaller sub-problems: spawn a prefab → point it at the player → move it through space → destroy it when done. Today, you read Unity's projectile functions and build Projectile.cs from scratch.

Read the Docs ~15 min

Firing a projectile requires coordinating several distinct Unity functions. Read how the engine handles each step:

Sub-ProblemUnity FunctionDocumentation & Purpose
1. Spawning Instantiate(prefab, pos, rot) Creates a brand-new clone of a prefab at runtime and places it into the scene hierarchy.
2. Aiming (target - origin).normalized Vector subtraction produces a vector pointing toward the target. .normalized reduces its length to 1.
3. Moving transform.Translate or Rigidbody2D Moves the bullet every frame along its forward direction.
4. Cleanup Destroy(gameObject, delay) Destroys the projectile after a time delay (seconds) to prevent off-screen bullets from clogging memory.

Socratic: Evaluating Multiple Ways to Move Projectiles

Compare these two ways to move a projectile across the screen:

  • Method 1 (Translate): transform.Translate(Vector3.right * speed * Time.deltaTime);
  • Method 2 (Physics Velocity): GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>().linearVelocity = direction * speed;
  1. If you want bullets that bounce off stone walls like in a pinball or billiards game, which method (Method 1 or Method 2) is significantly easier, and why?
  2. If your projectiles are laser beams, energy arrows, or magic missiles that fly straight through obstacles, why is Method 1 clean and lightweight?
  3. Why is Destroy(gameObject, 5f) called an essential garbage collection pattern? What would happen to your game's framerate if a player dodged 1,000 bullets and they all kept flying into deep space forever?
Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — Build Projectile.cs from scratch. In Assets/Scripts/, create a new C# script named Projectile.cs:

using UnityEngine;

public class Projectile : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float speed = 6f;
    [SerializeField] private float lifetime = 4f;

    public void Initialize(Vector3 targetPosition)
    {
        // 1. Calculate direction toward the target
        Vector3 direction = (targetPosition - transform.position).normalized;

        // 2. Rotate the sprite so its right side faces the target
        float angle = Mathf.Atan2(direction.y, direction.x) * Mathf.Rad2Deg;
        transform.rotation = Quaternion.AngleAxis(angle, Vector3.forward);

        // 3. Schedule automatic cleanup after lifetime seconds
        Destroy(gameObject, lifetime);
    }

    private void Update()
    {
        // Fly forward along its rotated local right vector
        transform.Translate(Vector3.right * speed * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}

In Assets/Prefabs/, select the Turret_Projectile prefab and attach your new Projectile.cs script to it.

Step 2 — Add AttackPlayer to TurretController.cs. Open TurretController.cs. Declare slots for the projectile prefab and spawn point, then write AttackPlayer():

    [SerializeField] private GameObject projectilePrefab;
    [SerializeField] private Transform projectileSpawnPoint;

    private void AttackPlayer()
    {
        if (projectilePrefab == null || projectileSpawnPoint == null) return;

        // Spawn projectile at muzzle position with no initial rotation
        GameObject proj = Instantiate(projectilePrefab, projectileSpawnPoint.position, Quaternion.identity);

        // Aim and fire at player's current position
        proj.GetComponent<Projectile>().Initialize(playerTransform.position);
    }

Step 3 — Wire the Inspector slots.

  1. Select the Turret in the Overworld scene.
  2. Drag Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile into the Projectile Prefab slot.
  3. In the Hierarchy, expand the Turret GameObject to find its child projectileSpawnPoint, and drag it into the Projectile Spawn Point slot.

In TurretController.Update(), call AttackPlayer(); inside your range check: 

        if (distanceToPlayer <= maxAttackRange)
        {
            AttackPlayer();
        }

Save and press Play. Walk near the turret. A projectile spawns from the muzzle, aims at your position, and shoots across the screen! (Notice that it fires 60 bullets every second — in lesson 3.3a we fix the cooldown!)

Bug Hunt: Projectile Errors

  1. What happens if you leave the Projectile Prefab slot unassigned in the Inspector? What error does Unity throw when you step in range?
  2. In Projectile.cs, what happens if you change Vector3.right to Vector3.up in Update()? Which direction do bullets fly relative to their aim?
  3. In Projectile.cs, comment out the Destroy(gameObject, lifetime) line. Fire several bullets and watch the Hierarchy in play mode. Do the spawned instances ever leave the scene?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Bullet Tuning

  1. In the Turret_Projectile prefab, tune speed between 3 (slow dodgeable dodgeball) and 15 (bullet-hell sniper). How does projectile speed alter the player's emotional reaction to the turret?
  2. Why does Initialize calculate the direction once, instead of continuously updating direction in Update()? What kind of weapon would you get if direction re-aimed toward the player every frame?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break down projectile firing into instantiation, aiming, translation, and destruction
  • Explain the role of Instantiate() in stamping runtime prefab clones
  • Explain why vectors are normalized before calculating angle and movement
  • Create Projectile.cs and wire the turret's projectile spawn slots
  • Commit your projectile system to GitHub
